newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Kiwi airline loses battle for survival.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kiwi airline loses battle for survival.

text.p: Budget carrier Kiwi International collapsed on Monday with the loss of more than 250 jobs after a young New Zealand businessman failed in a David and Goliath battle with Australasia's most powerful airlines.

Kiwi chief executive Ewan Wilson, a former travel agent who had taken on Qantas Airways and Air New Zealand in the cut-throat budget air travel market, admitted defeat after a series of crushing setbacks.

"We tried very, very hard to run an airline that was competitive and sustainable. I don't think we should hold our head low," Wilson, 30, told a news conference to announce the airline's voluntary liquidation.

Operating with two leased aircraft, Kiwi had run up to 30 flights a week between New Zealand and Australia, but was hurt by severe competition, mechanical faults and flight disruptions from the eruption of Mount Ruapehu volcano in the North Island.
The last straw was a legal dispute with Singapore's Region Air, lessor of an A320 Airbus that was grounded at Brisbane airport last week because of differences over lease terms.

"I think we have achieved a great deal in two and a half years. We have moved more than 230,000 passengers safely and affordably across the Tasman and employed over 200 people who may not have had jobs otherwise," Wilson said.
Wilson, who founded and owned 48 percent of Kiwi, had planned a NZ$15-20 million (US$10.4-13.9 million) float and set his sights on expansion to new destinations such as Singapore.
"This is an illustration of what happens to a company that expands too rapidly, mixed with a great deal of environmental and other factors that have made life very tough," Wilson said.

Kiwi's two leased planes were grounded in Christchurch and Brisbane, leaving passengers stranded. Television New Zealand said those waiting in Brisbane included a group of psychiatric patients and a brass band from Dunedin in the South Island.

Australia's Qantas offered special one-way fares to help passengers get home. Air New Zealand, which launched its own budget-charter operation, Freedom Air, to meet the threat from Kiwi, said it would continue offering bargain fares.
"The end of Kiwi doesn't mean the end of cut prices at all. The consumers want them. There is a market there, clearly someone's going to be feeding it," spokesman David Beatson said.

Liquidator John Waller of Price Waterhouse said it was too early to comment on the size of Kiwi's debts. Legal issues to be examined included lease arrangements with Region Air, which Kiwi had last week threatened to sue for damages.

"Obviously there will be unsecured creditors and there will be a number of people who have pre-paid for travel that they had not commenced, but at this stage we are not sure what that number is," Waller said.
But staff and customers in Kiwi's home base, the North Island town of Hamilton, appeared to sympathise with the young entreprenuer.

"Somebody should help him out, like some of these big airlines, instead of digging the knife in and letting him go under," said Janet Dix, a Hamilton woman who was $825 out of pocket after pre-paying for tickets to Australia in Kiwi's budget "peanuts and cola" class.
